name: At-home fractional laser

lead: At-home fractional lasers are low-energy, non-ablative handhelds that treat the skin in a grid of microscopic zones, leaving the tissue between them untouched. People use them for a smoother texture, softer fine lines and mild scarring on the face.

Each tiny zone of controlled heat injury triggers wound healing and new collagen, so changes build gradually across sessions. Clinic fractional lasers have a large research literature, including studies on atrophic and acne scars; home devices are gentler, and a 2026 review of home devices grouped fractional lasers with LED and radiofrequency as categories with a favorable efficacy-safety balance.

paras: Users pass the device over the face in a set pattern on a regular schedule, usually in the evening, with sun protection the next day. It is typically added to an existing routine of cleanser, moisturizer and sunscreen, and visible change is described as gradual over repeated sessions.

Possible effects include redness, dryness, temporary pigment change and, with misuse, burns or infection. Sun protection and skin-type suitability matter. Results are gentler than clinic procedures, and evidence varies by device because no systematic review has focused only on home fractional lasers.

angle.text: Tiny zones of controlled skin injury prompt collagen remodelling, which smooths texture and softens fine lines and mild scars as sessions add up. Clinic fractional lasers are well studied; home versions are lower in energy and vary by device.

lead: An at-home fractional laser is a handheld, low-energy, typically non-ablative device that delivers light to the skin in a grid of tiny zones, leaving surrounding tissue untouched. Consumer versions are sold for fine lines, uneven texture and mild scarring on the face, and are lower-powered relatives of clinic fractional resurfacing.

The clinic technology has a substantial literature. Fractional photothermolysis with a 1,550 nm erbium fibre laser was studied for atrophic scars in 2007, a consensus report addressed ablative fractional resurfacing for traumatic scars in 2014, and systematic reviews have examined fractional CO2 lasers for depressed acne scars.[1][2][3] Home devices have a much thinner evidence base.

A 2026 review of home-based dermatologic devices for acne and rejuvenation and a 2022 systematic review of home-based dermatology devices are the main overviews; the latter included 37 studies of 16 devices, and found no double-blinded randomized trials among them.[4][5] The 2022 review's laser findings concerned hair growth in androgenic alopecia and not fractional skin resurfacing.[5]

For appearance, the idea is gradual skin renewal at home: repeated low-energy sessions meant to smooth fine lines and surface texture, with fewer days of redness and downtime than a clinic procedure.[5][6]
infobox: Strong for clinic lasers; limited for home units

paras: Wikipedia credits R. Rox Anderson, of the Wellman Center for Photomedicine, as inventor of the patent that Reliant Technologies licensed to launch the Fraxel fractional line in 2004.[7] Fraxel Restore uses a 1,550 nm erbium glass non-ablative laser, Fraxel Restore Dual adds a 1,927 nm thulium fibre laser, and Fraxel Repair uses an ablative 10,600 nm CO2 laser.[7]

A 2020 review notes that many non-ablative devices appeared during the 2000s, aiming to improve skin appearance with less downtime and fewer complications than older resurfacing; most used fractional delivery, leaving islands of untreated skin between treated areas, which was thought to speed healing.[8] Consumer lower-energy versions followed that idea.

Fractional lasers split the beam into many microscopic columns of thermal injury. Clinic devices are divided into ablative systems, such as CO2 lasers that vaporise tissue columns, and non-ablative systems, such as 1,550 nm erbium-doped fibre lasers, which heat without removing tissue.[1][3] Home devices use the non-ablative approach at much lower energy, so treatments are repeated over time. Reviews of energy-based devices in skin of colour note non-ablative fractional lasers target water rather than melanin, which is described as safer for darker skin types.

The accepted model is that the microscopic injury columns trigger wound healing and new collagen production in the surrounding intact tissue, while the faster healing allows shorter recovery than fully ablative resurfacing. A 2011 editorial introduced fractional laser resurfacing in this way.[6]

Home users treat the face, and sometimes the neck or hands, in repeated passes over several weeks, hoping for smoother texture, softened fine lines and a better look to shallow scars, with a few days of pinkness rather than the longer recovery of a clinic procedure.[5][7] Because home devices deliver less energy than clinic systems, results are described as gradual, and clinic non-ablative lasers are themselves typically given in a series.[8]

Dermatology reviews describe skin type, recent sun exposure and active infection such as herpes as factors that affect risk after fractional resurfacing, and describe sun protection as part of aftercare.[9][10]

In clinic settings, a 2022 meta-analysis of six articles with 467 patients found ultra-pulsed CO2 fractional laser scored higher for skin smoothness than comparator methods in depressed acne scars.[1] A 2007 study applied 1,550 nm fractional photothermolysis to atrophic scars.[3] A 2020 randomized split-face study and other trials examined combinations with exosomes, microneedling radiofrequency and poly-L-lactic acid.[11][12][13]

For home devices, a 2022 review of home-based dermatology devices found laser evidence mainly for hair regrowth and RF evidence for wrinkles, and concluded that home devices appeared safe and effective for several uses but that trials were few, unblinded or short.[5] A 2026 review of home-based devices for acne and rejuvenation is reported to rank fractional lasers, LED and radiofrequency among categories with the best balance of efficacy and safety; its abstract could not be examined in full.[4] No systematic review focused solely on home fractional lasers was identified.

A 2010 review of complications of fractionated laser resurfacing and a study of 961 treatments catalogue side effects of clinic procedures, which include erythema, edema, pigment change, infection and scarring in the professional setting.[9][10] Home devices deliver less energy and carry a lower expected risk, but misuse, unsuitable skin types and inadequate sun protection are recognised concerns in dermatology reviews.[9]

Wikipedia's overview of laser skin resurfacing describes photorejuvenation with lasers, intense pulsed light and photodynamic therapy. Laser types include erbium:glass at 1,540 nm (non-ablative), erbium:YAG at 2,940 nm and CO2 at 10,600 nm (both ablative). Ablative resurfacing vaporises tissue and creates wounds, while non-ablative treatment leaves the surface intact; in both, heating the deeper dermis is described as stimulating fibroblasts to form new collagen and elastin.[14]

Fractional lasers deliver hundreds or thousands of pinpoints per square inch and leave healthy skin between the treated spots, and the same article describes erbium and CO2 fractional systems as having a better safety profile than older full-surface lasers.[14] It credits Thomas L. Roberts III with inventing CO2 resurfacing techniques in the 1990s and lists scarring, hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks among observed adverse effects, with CO2 carrying a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers because it generates more heat.[14]

The 2022 systematic review of home-based dermatology devices searched PubMed, Embase and CINAHL in November 2020 and included 37 studies with 1,871 patients: 19 randomised trials, 16 case series and two non-randomised trials.[5] It covered intense pulsed light for hair removal, laser diodes for androgenic alopecia, radiofrequency for wrinkles, LED for acne and UVB for psoriasis, and microneedling was not included.[5]

For wrinkles the evidence was radiofrequency: one randomised trial of a home eyebrow-lifting device reported a reduction in eyebrow-to-hairline distance of up to 1.52 cm after one treatment, and a 12-week non-randomised study of 45 patients reported better elasticity and firmness with painless treatment.[5] The authors judged all device types to have favourable safety profiles with few significant adverse events, such as mild transient redness, and listed as limitations the small number of trials, the absence of double-blind placebo-controlled studies and short follow-up.[5]

Clinic-based trials and meta-analyses of fractional lasers are extensive for acne scars, hypertrophic scars and melasma.[1][2][15] For home-use fractional lasers specifically, evidence is limited to broad reviews of home devices that did not isolate them.[4][5]
The 2022 review summarised above is the main body of research on home devices, with its laser findings focused on hair growth and its wrinkle findings on radiofrequency.[5]

lore.intro: Home fractional lasers are discussed in skincare circles as a lower-cost, lower-downtime version of clinic resurfacing for texture, fine lines and shallow scars.[5][6]
